title: How do you read a waterfall chart in a case interview?
description: How waterfall charts show what moved a number from one value to another, how to read them quickly, the common traps, and a worked profit bridge.
hook: Waterfall charts, sometimes called bridge charts, are a consultant favourite because they answer the question every profit case asks: what changed? Once you know how to read one, they are among the fastest charts to draw an insight from.
body:
What it shows

A starting value on the left, an ending value on the right, and floating bars in between showing each increase or decrease. Together they explain the change.

A worked example

Profit went from £10M to £7M. The bars in between: price +£1M, volume −£0.5M, ingredients −£1.5M, wages −£1M, energy −£1M. Check they add up: 10 + 1 − 0.5 − 1.5 − 1 − 1 = 7. ✓

Insight: "Costs explain the whole fall: £3.5M of extra costs, led by ingredients, more than offset a £1M gain from price. I'd look at ingredients first."

How to read one in 30 seconds

  1. Read the start and end values, and the size of the change.
  2. Find the biggest bar, up or down.
  3. Group the bars: revenue drivers versus cost drivers.
  4. Say what explains most of the change, and what to look at next.

Common traps

  • Describing every bar in order instead of leading with the biggest.
  • Missing that small bars add up: three small cost increases can matter more than one big one.
  • Not checking units and time period.

Work backwards from the gap the client needs explained

Imagine a retailer's operating profit fell from £10 million to £7 million. The waterfall begins at £10 million, shows an extra £1 million from higher prices, then subtracts £2 million from lower sales volumes and another £2 million from higher logistics costs. The bridge reconciles: £10m + £1m − £2m − £2m = £7m. If the bars did not add to £7 million, check whether a category, adjustment or sign is missing before explaining the chart.

The point is not to read each bar aloud. The client needs to know which factors caused the decline and which are actionable. Here, volume and logistics are equally large negative contributors, while price partly offsets them. Ask whether volume loss is concentrated in a particular region or customer group, and whether logistics inflation reflects higher supplier prices or inefficient deliveries. Those are different interventions.

A subtle trap is double counting. A price-volume bridge may include a separate interaction term when price and quantity both change. Do not independently calculate a price effect on the new volume and a volume effect on the new price unless you deliberately account for that interaction. Say which baseline you are using.

Try it aloud: "Profit is down £3 million. The two main negatives are £2 million each from volume and logistics, partly offset by £1 million from pricing. I'd investigate what changed in demand and cost per delivery before choosing a response." That is a useful interpretation, not a description of a picture.
